planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, gritty, sandy soil in full sun; 'Smithwick' is propagated only from pads to preserve its named-selection traits.

directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; this low, mat-forming selection was found near Smithwick, South Dakota and introduced by prairie-plant collector Claude Barr for its exceptional cold hardiness and prolific bloom. Flattened blue-green pads stay low and spreading, rarely exceeding 8 inches tall, and are topped in late spring with unusually large, silky yellow flowers with red centers that appear more freely than on many wild eastern prickly pear populations. It survives northern Great Plains winters with minimal dieback and needs no supplemental irrigation once established. Handle pads with heavy gloves, since fine glochids detach easily on contact even though large spines are sparse.
scientific_name_note: A Claude Barr selection of hybrid origin (believed Opuntia fragilis x O. polyacantha lineage), commonly sold and grown as a cold-hardy Opuntia humifusa-type prickly pear.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end an inch into very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; hairspine pricklypear roots readily from single pad cuttings.

directions: Plant a callused pad in very well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; hairspine pricklypear is among the most cold-hardy cacti in North America, native from the Canadian prairie provinces south through the Great Plains and Intermountain West into New Mexico and Arizona, where it survives winters to -40 degrees F by shrinking and wrinkling its pads. Flattened, blue-green to gray-green pads are densely armed with long, hair-fine spines (the source of the common name) and produce large, silky flowers in shades of pale yellow to magenta-pink in early summer, followed by dry, spiny, tan fruit. It spreads slowly into a low, sprawling colony well suited to dry slopes, rock gardens, and unirrigated high-plains xeriscape beds. Handle with heavy gloves, since the fine glochids embed readily and are difficult to remove.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or plant rooted offsets/transplants in spring into sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than soil fertility.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, rocky or gravelly, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; native to a limited range in Oklahoma, Kansas, and the Texas Panhandle, this variety of lace hedgehog cactus is even more cold-tolerant than the typical form, surviving winter lows well below zero Fahrenheit with essentially no damage when kept dry. Dense, interlacing white to pinkish spines cover small, clustering, cylindrical stems, and clumps produce large, satiny pink flowers with a pale throat in late spring. It is a favorite of cold-climate cactus and crevice-garden growers as far north as USDA zone 4, provided it is sited in sharply drained, gritty soil where winter moisture cannot pool around the roots. Rot from wet soil, not cold, is the greatest risk to this hardy variety in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; growth from seed to a landscape-sized barrel is slow, typically many years.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; native to the arid hills of Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, and San Luis Potosi in northeastern Mexico, this dramatic barrel cactus is prized for its dense covering of vivid red to orange-red spines that give young plants a fiery, glowing appearance rare among barrel cacti. Growth begins slowly as a squat globe but accelerates with age, and older specimens become tall, ribbed columns that may branch from the base into small clusters over many decades. Rings of magenta to yellow flowers appear at the crown in summer, followed by small yellow fruit. It tolerates only brief, light frost, so in zones 9a and cooler it should be grown in a container or sited in a warm, sheltered, south-facing microclimate with protection from prolonged winter wet.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Devil's Tongue Barrel Cactus (Broad-Spined Barrel Cactus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a sterile, mineral cactus mix, or set out nursery transplants in spring into very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; growth from seed to a mature flowering specimen takes many years.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gravelly or sandy, lean soil in full sun; native to the high plateaus of central Mexico, this compact, solitary, globe- to barrel-shaped cactus is named for its broad, flattened, downward-hooking red to yellow central spine that resembles a curved tongue jutting from each areole. Unlike most barrel cacti, it often flowers in late fall or early winter rather than summer, producing a ring of pink to purple-red blooms at the crown, earning it the nickname 'birthday cactus' among growers in some regions. It tolerates brief dips into the upper teens Fahrenheit once established in lean, sharply drained soil, but prolonged freezes or wet winter soil quickly cause fatal rot, so in zones 9a and cooler it should be grown in a container or sited in a warm, sheltered microclimate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Emory's barrel cactus has a naturally limited range and is best sourced from nursery-propagated stock rather than wild-collected plants.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, rocky, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; established plants need no supplemental irrigation in low-desert climates. Ferocactus emoryi has the most limited native range of the large barrel cacti in the United States, found only in a small area of far southern Arizona centered on Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument and extending into Sonora, Sinaloa, and Baja California Sur, Mexico. A large, cylindrical to columnar cactus with 15 to 30 ribs armed with dense clusters of reddish to reddish-gray, slightly curved spines, it produces rings of red to yellow flowers at the crown from July through September, later than many other barrel cacti. Extremely slow-growing and long-lived, it makes a striking architectural specimen for a hot, low-desert xeriscape but is more cold-sensitive than the widespread fishhook barrel cactus (Ferocactus wislizeni), so it should be reserved for the warmest low-desert gardens.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, filtered light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; silken pincushion cactus needs excellent drainage and colors and clusters best with strong but not scorching light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright, filtered light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; silken pincushion cactus needs excellent drainage and rots quickly if left in wet soil. Slender, cylindrical stems are densely covered in fine, silky white radial spines interspersed with a few longer, golden to reddish-brown hooked central spines, giving the plant a soft, glowing halo pierced by a scattering of stouter, hooked spines. Native to Jalisco in west-central Mexico, it offsets readily from the base to form a dense, mounding cluster of stems within a few years, and mature clumps produce a ring of pink to magenta-pink flowers near the crown in spring. Water only when the soil is fully dry, give a cooler, drier winter rest to encourage the following season's bloom, and separate offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Sea Urchin Cactus (Pink Easter Lily Cactus)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; sea urchin cactus flowers most reliably with strong but filtered light and a distinct winter rest.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining cactus mix; sea urchin cactus needs excellent drainage and benefits from strong but filtered light rather than harsh, baking full sun. Native to Uruguay, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, and Paraguay, this fast-growing, globose to short-cylindrical cactus offsets readily from the base to form a wide, showy clump within a few seasons, easily the most popular and easiest-to-grow Echinopsis for beginners. Large, sweetly fragrant, funnel-shaped white to pink flowers up to 4 inches across open in late afternoon and evening in late spring and summer, then wither by the next afternoon, often appearing in flushes of several blooms at once on a well-grown clump. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide a cool 50-55 degree F winter rest to encourage the following season's flowers, and separate rooted offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
